config.title: HTTP from scratch

intro.title: HTTP from scratch
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a basic HTTP server from scratch using only Node.js core modules, without any external frameworks. You will learn the core concept of how HTTP servers handle incoming requests and send back responses. The main technologies involved are the Node.js 'http' module, request and response objects, and basic networking. By the end, you will understand how to create a server that listens on a port and responds to client requests, forming the foundation of web development in Node.js.
intro.usecase: Understanding HTTP from scratch is essential when building custom web servers, APIs, or middleware in Node.js. This foundational knowledge is applied in real products like payment gateway integrations, where precise control over request/response cycles is required, or in monitoring dashboards that aggregate data from multiple HTTP endpoints. Developers use these low-level HTTP skills to optimize performance in high-traffic applications, debug network issues in production systems, and implement custom authentication or logging layers that standard frameworks don't provide.

objectives: Construct a basic HTTP server using Node.js's built-in http module
Initialize server configuration to handle incoming requests on a specified port
Manipulate HTTP response objects to send appropriate status codes and headers
Implement request handlers to process different HTTP methods (GET, POST)
Configure routing logic to direct requests to specific endpoints
Integrate request parsing to extract data from URL parameters and request bodies
Control server lifecycle by properly starting and stopping the HTTP server

steps.title: Import the Node.js HTTP module
steps.instruction: Import the HTTP module using require('http')
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import the built-in 'http' module and assign it to a variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing another built-in module
const fs = require('fs');
steps.expectedOutcome: The HTTP module is imported and ready to use for creating a server.
successCriteria: The 'http' module is imported using require('http') and assigned to a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using require('http') to import the module and assigning it to a variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to use require('http') to import the HTTP module.

steps.title: Create a basic HTTP server
steps.instruction: Create an HTTP server using the imported HTTP module's createServer method and store it in a variable named 'server'.
steps.hint: Call http.createServer() and assign the result to a const variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating a server instance
const server = http.createServer();
steps.seedCode:
const http = require('http');

// Create an HTTP server here
steps.expectedOutcome: A server variable is declared and initialized with the result of http.createServer().
successCriteria: A variable named 'server' is declared using const and assigned the value returned by http.createServer().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created an HTTP server instance.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the imported 'http' module and storing the result in a variable named 'server'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server wasn't created correctly. Check that you're calling http.createServer() and assigning it to a const variable named 'server'.

steps.title: Define the request handler callback function
steps.instruction: Define a function named 'requestHandler' that takes 'req' and 'res' as parameters. The function body can be empty for now.
steps.hint: Create a function that will handle incoming HTTP requests. Use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'requestHandler' with 'req' and 'res' parameters is defined, ready to be used as the server callback.
successCriteria: The code contains a function named 'requestHandler' that accepts two parameters (req and res).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named 'requestHandler' and accepts two parameters (req and res).
steps.feedbackWrong: define a function named 'requestHandler' that takes 'req' and 'res' as parameters.

steps.title: Set response headers for plain text
steps.instruction: Inside your request handler callback function, use response.writeHead() to set the status code to 200 and the Content-Type header to 'text/plain'.
steps.hint: The writeHead() method takes two arguments: the status code and an object containing headers. For plain text responses, set Content-Type to 'text/plain'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will respond with proper HTTP headers indicating a successful plain text response.
successCriteria: The request handler uses response.writeHead() with status code 200 and Content-Type: 'text/plain'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're using writeHead() with both the status code and headers object. Make sure Content-Type is set to 'text/plain'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The headers aren't set correctly. Remember to use response.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' }) inside your request handler.

steps.title: Write response body content
steps.instruction: Inside the requestHandler function, after setting the response headers, use response.end() to send the text 'Hello from Node.js HTTP server!' as the response body.
steps.hint: The response.end() method sends the response body and ends the response. Pass your message string as the first argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The request handler will now send a complete HTTP response with both headers and body content.
successCriteria: The requestHandler function includes response.end() with the specified text message as argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling response.end() with the exact text message 'Hello from Node.js HTTP server!' inside the requestHandler function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the requestHandler function, after the writeHead call, add response.end('Hello from Node.js HTTP server!');

steps.title: Make the server listen on a port
steps.instruction: Call the server.listen() method on your server instance, passing port 3000 and a callback function that logs a message when the server starts.
steps.hint: Use server.listen(3000, () => { console.log('Server running on port 3000'); })
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will be configured to start listening for incoming HTTP requests on port 3000, with a confirmation message logged to the console.
successCriteria: server.listen() is called with port 3000 and a callback function that logs a startup message
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're calling server.listen() with both the port number (3000) and a callback function that logs a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: call the listen() method on your server instance with port 3000 and a callback function.

steps.title: Add console log for server startup
steps.instruction: Inside the listen callback function, add a console.log() statement to print a message confirming the server is running.
steps.hint: The callback function receives an error parameter first, but you can ignore it for now and just log a success message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will log a message to the console when it successfully starts listening on port 3000.
successCriteria: A console.log() statement is added inside the listen callback function with a success message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a console.log() but it might be in the wrong place. Make sure it's inside the listen callback function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The console.log() statement is missing or not inside the listen callback. Try adding console.log('Server running on port 3000') inside the callback.

steps.title: Handle different URL paths
steps.instruction: Inside the requestHandler function, add an if statement to check if request.url equals '/' and send a different response for the root path.
steps.hint: Use request.url to get the requested URL path. Compare it with '/' using strict equality (===). Inside the if block, write a response for the root path before calling response.end().
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now respond with 'Welcome to the homepage!' only when the root URL (/) is accessed, while other URLs will still show the default message.
successCriteria: The requestHandler function contains an if statement that checks request.url === '/' and writes a specific response for that path.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking request.url with strict equality (===) and writing the response inside the if block.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional logic for URL handling isn't quite right. Remember to check request.url === '/' and write a response specifically for that path.

steps.title: Add a 404 Not Found handler
steps.instruction: In your requestHandler function, add an else clause after your existing if statement to handle all other URLs with a 404 status and 'Not Found' message.
steps.hint: After your if block that checks for '/', add an else block that sets the status to 404 and writes 'Not Found' to the response.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your server will now properly respond with a 404 status and 'Not Found' message for any URL that isn't the homepage.
successCriteria: The requestHandler includes an else clause that sets status 404 and writes 'Not Found' to the response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your else clause sets the status to 404 and writes 'Not Found' to the response. Check that it comes after your if statement for '/'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The 404 handler isn't quite right. You need to add an else clause after your existing if statement that handles all other URLs by setting status 404 and writing 'Not Found'.

steps.title: Test the server with different requests
steps.instruction: Run your server by executing the file with Node.js,
steps.hint: Open your terminal, navigate to your project directory, and run 'node your-filename.js'. Then open a browser or use 'curl http://localhost:3000' in another terminal window.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your server should start successfully and respond with 'Welcome to the homepage!' for the root URL and '404 Not Found' for other URLs.
successCriteria: The server runs without errors and responds correctly to different URL paths when tested.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Your server runs, but check if it responds correctly to both the root URL and other paths. Make sure your conditional logic is properly implemented.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server doesn't start or respond correctly. Check your code for syntax errors and ensure the request handler properly handles different URL paths.
